title: New AI agent observability and governance across BigQuery and Looker
raw_text: As enterprises move AI agents from experimental prototypes into production, data and platform teams are discovering that deploying an agent is only half the battle — you also need to see how it reasons, which data it touches, and what it costs to run. Today, we are announcing expanded AI agent observability and evaluation capabilities across Google Data Cloud, giving you unified visibility into your first-party (1P) data agents in BigQuery and Looker as well as custom third-party (3P) agents built with agent development frameworks such as Agent Development Kit (ADK) or LangGraph. Putting conversational and autonomous agents into production requires solving three operational challenges: tracing multi-step reasoning while protecting sensitive data, controlling token consumption and query spend, and evaluating answer accuracy before prompt or schema changes reach users. Let’s explore how our new agent observability and evaluation capabilities help you do this. What's new: Agent observability across Data Cloud Running agents at scale means you need to see how they perform, what they cost, and what actions they take. We're rolling out a unified telemetry framework across Google's Agentic Data Cloud that works the same way for every agent: Capture telemetry from the agent, land it in BigQuery tables you own, and analyze it wherever your teams already work. Unified agent observability framework capturing logging telemetry across 1P and 3P agents into BigQuery to surface performance and usage insights across developer and admin tools. 1. Capture telemetry from every first-party and custom agent First-party data agents: Out-of-the-box Conversational Analytics agents emit telemetry automatically with no setup required. Queries routed to BigQuery data agents in Gemini Enterprise through agent-to-agent (A2A) workflows (now GA) send Cloud Monitoring metrics, Cloud Trace spans, and BigQuery conversation logs straight into your agent's project. Custom agents: Agents built with ADK or LangGraph stream the same structured telemetry into BigQuery through single-line SDK instrumentation. 2. Land telemetry in one governed home in BigQuery Conversation logging in BigQuery (GA): Managed 1P conversation logging writes to BigQuery tables you own, so you can inspect Conversational Analytics traces, including prompts and responses, directly in your data warehouse. Governed by default: The Conversational Analytics API , now GA, includes always-on admin audit logs and optional data-read audit logs in Cloud Audit Logs , and supports VPC Service Controls, customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), and regional and multi-regional data residency . 3. Analyze with dashboards wherever your teams work In BigQuery (GA): Agent monitoring provides prebuilt dashboards in BigQuery Studio to track usage, active sessions, top knowledge sources, and latency across BigQuery Conversational Analytics agents. BigQuery Conversational Analytics dashboard in BigQuery Studio, giving admins visibility into usage, active sessions, top knowledge sources, and latency. In Looker (GA): System Activity dashboards for Conversational Analytics, now GA in Looker (Google Cloud core) and Looker (original), track engagement and token usage, while user ratings and query review in the Responses & feedback tab are in preview. Looker Conversational Analytics dashboard in System Activity, giving admins visibility into usage, token consumption, and user feedback. Build your own: Create interactive reports with the open-source Data Studio template or deploy the ready-made Looker Block for Agent Analytics for real-time custom agent monitoring. Custom Data Studio dashboard built on BigQuery Agent Analytics logs to track token consumption, latency, and user engagement. Looker Block dashboard built on BigQuery Agent Analytics telemetry to monitor session volumes, tool execution latency, and token cost distribution. Tracing agent reasoning and protecting privacy Enterprise observability requires balancing diagnostic telemetry with strict data privacy boundaries. Because tracking features involve ingestion and storage costs, Google Data Cloud separates operational telemetry from conversation content so admins and agent owners can govern each layer independently. At the project or organization level, admins can enable Cloud Monitoring (aggregate metrics such as request volume, latency, and token usage) and Cloud Trace (step-by-step spans for each request) across their environment, using Cloud Trace observability scopes to consolidate telemetry across multiple agent projects. To protect sensitive data, these operational metrics and sanitized first-party trace spans exclude customer core content (such as user prompts, model responses, internal thoughts, and generated SQL). When you need deeper transcript auditing, agent owners and editors can opt in to conversation logging on a per-agent basis: Governed conversation logging in BigQuery: When enabled, a Google-managed service agent streams user prompts, responses, and turn-level telemetry into a customer-owned BigQuery table ( agent_events ) via the BigQuery Storage Write API, inheriting your dataset's IAM permissions, CMEK, and VPC Service Controls. Built-in privacy guardrails enforce a fail-closed check before each turn — skipping logging whenever a knowledge source uses row-level security, column-level policy tags, or dynamic data masking — while fail-open execution keeps your users' chat sessions uninterrupted if a logging error occurs. Full trace trees for custom 3P agents: While 1P conversation logging intentionally strips low-level tool arguments and internal SQL, developers building custom agents on ADK or LangGraph can instrument their code with the open-source ADK plugin ( BigQueryAgentAnalyticsPlugin ). With a single-line setup, the SDK streams full tool-invocation execution trees, time-series telemetry, and multimodal payloads straight into BigQuery. In-warehouse root cause and drift analysis: Because conversation logs land natively in your agent_events table, you don't need separate export pipelines to diagnose failures. You can run BigQuery AI functions (such as AI.GENERATE to summarize error patterns and AI.EMBED with VECTOR_SEARCH to cluster recurring issues) or use the open-source bigquery-agent-analytics Python SDK and Colab starter notebook for post-hoc semantic drift clustering and LLM-as-a-judge sentiment analysis. Controlling token costs with FinOps guardrails As agent adoption grows, FinOps and platform teams need clear visibility into consumption alongside active controls to prevent runaway spend. With promotional trial pricing currently available for Conversational Analytics, now is a good time to establish baseline usage and cost guardrails: Granular token and latency tracking: In BigQuery conversation logs, each turn records input, output, thought, cached, and total token counts alongside total turn latency, while Looker System Activity reports estimated input and output tokens across your business intelligence (BI) workloads. Turnkey observability dashboards: You can track projected token usage and engagement in the BigQuery Studio Monitoring tab and native Looker System Activity dashboards, or query agent_events log data via BigQuery SQL using the open-source seven-page Data Studio report template and self-hosted Streamlit app in the BigQuery Agent Analytics GitHub repository . Active query and token spend caps: To prevent unexpected charges before they happen, you can configure per-query BigQuery byte scan caps ( big_query_max_billed_bytes ) on your agent, which use dry-run estimates to block oversized queries without incurring on-demand scan charges. For BigQuery and the Conversational Analytics API, you can also enforce daily input and output token quotas (in preview) per project, user, or agent in the Google Cloud console and gcloud CLI. Evaluating and benchmarking your AI agents Runtime observability works alongside systematic evaluation. While logs and traces tell you how an agent behaved in production, evaluation benchmarks verify whether updates to your prompts, models, or data schemas improve SQL accuracy and answer quality before users experience a regression: Benchmarking with Prism: Our open-source evaluation tool, Prism , lets you test Conversational Analytics agents grounded in BigQuery tables or Looker Explores via the Conversational Analytics API using reusable test suites, regex assertions, and multi-region agent discovery (deployed behind an access layer such as Cloud IAP). Unified evaluation and production analytics: Prism can stream completed evaluation runs directly into day-partitioned BigQuery tables in your project, placing your pre-deployment benchmark scores right alongside your production agent_events logs for side-by-side analysis in BigQuery and Looker. Native BigQuery evaluations: First-party agent evaluations in BigQuery (built on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform evaluation service with bring-your-own-service-account support) are available in preview via API and a guided Colab notebook. Getting started Ready to bring visibility, governance, and cost control to your AI agents? Here is how to get started in three steps: Enable first-party agent observability. Turn on Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Trace in your project and opt in to per-agent conversation logging using the BigQuery agent monitoring guide , and track BI token consumption with the Looker Conversational Analytics overview and Looker System Activity documentation . Instrument custom agents and deploy analytics dashboards. Add the BigQuery Agent Analytics SDK to your ADK or LangGraph agents, launch the open-source Data Studio report template or Streamlit app, and explore in-warehouse log analysis with the Colab starter notebook . Benchmark your agents and set cost guardrails. Run automated accuracy suites with Prism , and configure BigQuery byte scan caps and daily token quotas via Manage BigQuery costs for agents .

title: Where supercomputing meets agentic AI: What’s new in Google Cloud HPC and AI at SC26
raw_text: Computational scientists and HPC engineers have always been among the earliest adopters of new computing paradigms, and agents are no exception. Today, research and engineering teams use AI models and agents for things such as ingesting dense scientific literature, optimizing code, and autonomously steering simulations. Yet moving from an agent that suggests code optimizations to an agentic system that reliably architects, provisions, and optimizes production HPC workloads at scale takes more than a general-purpose reasoning model. Without deep infrastructure and domain context, an unguided agent can still pair incompatible storage tiers with compute-optimized VMs, overlook placement policies, or stall when diagnosing a multi-node MPI fabric error. That challenge led our team to ask a simple question: What if we could package our deep HPC and scientific expertise into reusable agent skills, turning complex setup and optimization into guided workflows? At SC26, we are showing how Google Cloud brings agentic HPC to life with reusable skills that teach agents how to build and run HPC workloads. In addition, we’re also demonstrating evolutionary agents that optimize your algorithms at cloud scale, and purpose-built supercomputing infrastructure designed for where HPC meets AI. Teaching agents to speak HPC: From blueprints to skills Organizations rely on Cluster Toolkit to deploy repeatable, production-ready HPC environments on Google Cloud through declarative YAML blueprints. Now we are expanding these capabilities by pairing Cluster Toolkit with composable agent skills with self-describing, deterministic tools, validated through automated, end-to-end testing and available for download from the Google Skills and DeepMind Science Skills repositories. Together, this delivers: Infrastructure skills that validate before they deploy : When you ask an agent to stand up a cluster, the skill directs it to first audit your compute and storage quotas, run rapid canary checks for regional capacity, match your workload to a validated Cluster Toolkit blueprint, and wait for human approval, all before running the gcluster deploy command. Workload-specific skills that know the science : After your cluster is live, domain skills connected to Google Skills and DeepMind Science Skills guide the agent through things like configuring OpenFOAM and Siemens STAR-CCM+ fluid dynamics runs, tuning GROMACS and AlphaFold 3 life-sciences pipelines, or launching Devito and Open Porous Media (OPM) subsurface simulations with browser-based 3D visualization. Built-in governance and Day-2 diagnostics : Agents operate inside strict IAM, Kueue quota, and budget guardrails, with full provenance in Cloud Logging and structured troubleshooting skills ( gke-kueue-debugging ) to resolve stuck queues or node drains automatically. Scaling from local prototype to breakthrough code Configuring and running existing solvers is only part of the discovery loop. Across financial services, electronic design automation (EDA), manufacturing, logistics, pharmaceuticals, and AI training, competitive advantage comes from having the fastest underlying code and algorithms. Historically, squeezing out performance gains required scarce optimization specialists and costly brute-force compute. Developed by Google DeepMind, AlphaEvolve changes the equation by using a Gemini-powered evolutionary loop to iteratively mutate, benchmark, and optimize code and 3D engineering parameters against target metrics. The AlphaEvolve on Cloud Batch solution, streamlines the process of moving from a seed algorithm on a laptop to massive parallel experimentation. With Batch, you get: Automated parallel evaluation : A single gcluster blueprint provisions the AlphaEvolve controller environment and uses Batch to fan out hundreds of candidate evaluations concurrently across single-VM sandboxes or multi-node MPI task groups. Interactive control from your preferred surface : Researchers can steer evolutionary experiments and inspect candidate lineage through hosted Python notebooks, or integrate optimization runs directly into their existing CLI workloads and agent-driven development tools. Evaluation at production scale : Evolving an algorithm on a single node with slow networking risks producing code that only performs well at small scale. By evaluating candidates across Google Cloud compute instances with Cloud RDMA and Google Cloud Managed Lustre — and using Spot VMs or Dynamic Workload Scheduler (DWS) to balance cost against turnaround time — you discover algorithms tuned for real supercomputing fabrics, permanently lowering the compute cost of every future production run. Supercomputing infrastructure under the hood An autonomous workflow is only as capable as the infrastructure beneath it. As agentic pipelines pivot dynamically between memory-bandwidth-bound physics solvers, domain foundation models (like AlphaFold 3 , AlphaGenome , and WeatherNext ), and large-scale AI training, Google Cloud provides a unified hardware and orchestration fabric managed by Cluster Director that offers: Tightly coupled HPC and scale-out compute : Run classic MPI simulations on H4D instances powered by 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors and Cloud RDMA, including 3 TB high-memory shapes built for large EDA and engineering models. Alternatively, you can maximize performance-per-watt on Arm-based C4A instances powered by Google Axion. Next-generation GPU acceleration : Run coupled physics-AI pipelines and multi-node GPU simulations on A4 and A4X instances (NVIDIA Blackwell B200 and GB200 NVL72), scale frontier AI training and reasoning on newly available A5X bare metal instances built on the NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 platform, and use G4 instances with NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs to accelerate CAE, CFD, and 3D visualization while reducing per-core software licensing costs. 8th gen TPUs for the agentic era : Deploy 8th generation TPUs , featuring TPU 8t for large-scale pre-training, reinforcement learning, and accelerated mathematical modeling and simulation (ModSim), alongside TPU 8i for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning and agentic inference. Additionally, Batch now supports running jobs on single-host TPU slices , providing flexible provisioning options for accelerated HPC and AI/ML workloads. Sub-millisecond parallel storage : Reduce data bottlenecks between simulation and AI stages with Google Cloud Managed Lustre , delivering up to 10 TB/s of read throughput, GPUDirect Storage over RDMA, and an 80 PB Dynamic Tier with Cloud Storage Mirroring. For even more performance, you can pair it with Cloud Storage FUSE local SSD caching. Experience it live at SC26 in Chicago Agentic HPC is not about turning unguided models loose on a terminal. This shift is about combining the reasoning power of Gemini with the codified engineering of Cluster Toolkit skills, evolutionary optimization on Batch, and purpose-built supercomputing hardware — so your teams spend their time on discovery rather than infrastructure plumbing. title: From OLAP to OLTP: How Copel Simplified Reverse ETL Using BigQuery's Native Export to AlloyDB
raw_text:
Bridging the gap between analytical systems (OLAP) and transactional databases (OLTP) is notoriously complex. Synchronizing data between the two systems, often called Reverse ETL (Extract, Transform, Load), traditionally requires heavy middleware, staging buckets, and complex orchestration, especially at enterprise scale. We’re announcing the general availability (GA) of BigQuery exports to AlloyDB , allowing data engineering teams to use a single, declarative SQL statement to export data from BigQuery to AlloyDB. This approach completely removes the need for complex ETL middleware. To demonstrate the benefits of this feature, we are sharing how Copel , a Brazilian electric power provider, eliminated a massive orchestration bottleneck and scaled their smart meter telemetry by migrating to high-performance, built-in Reverse ETL. The challenge of scaling smart meter telemetry At Copel, managing telemetry data from millions of smart electricity meters is a mission-critical operation. This data is streamed continuously and consolidated in an analytical Gold layer in BigQuery. However, to power Copel's "Systems of Action" — low-latency customer support dashboards, mobile applications, and operational billing systems — this rich dataset must be constantly synced back into its high-performance transactional database, AlloyDB for PostgreSQL. Until recently, Copel orchestrated this Reverse ETL architecture with a complex DAG in Google’s Managed Service for Apache Airflow. However, there were multiple brittle, intermediate stages in the process of enriching and exporting hundreds of millions of records from BigQuery to AlloyDB: Figure 1: Copel’s legacy multi-stage architecture requiring Cloud Storage file dumps and sequential gCloud scripts. BigQuery ran enrichment and extraction queries, dumping SQL results into dozens of fragmented CSV files inside a Google Cloud Storage bucket. Apache Airflow executed SQL to create temp tables in AlloyDB to prevent write locking or data corruption for production tables. Sequential gCloud scripts combed through the Cloud Storage CSVs to load data into a respective AlloyDB cluster and shards. Finally, a SQL transaction block safely dropped the production table and renamed the temporary table to production. To run this legacy architecture, Copel’s team needed to maintain the pipeline, carefully manage file staging, perform complex IAM impersonation across multiple services, and constantly monitor end-to-end system health. The breakthrough: Built-in Reverse ETL With BigQuery's EXPORT DATA to AlloyDB , Copel was able to replace this entire multi-step pipeline infrastructure with a single, elegant SQL statement. Now, BigQuery exports communicate directly with AlloyDB instances over highly optimized, parallelized connections — no staging files in Cloud Storage, gCloud scripts, or managing temporary tables required! Figure 2: New architecture showing direct parallel Reverse ETL connection between BigQuery and AlloyDB. Here is how simple the new Reverse ETL process looks in code: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'EXPORT DATA
 WITH CONNECTION `project_id.location.connection_id`
 OPTIONS(
 format='ALLOYDB',
 uri="https://alloydb.googleapis.com/v1/projects/my-project/locations/my-location/clusters/my-cluster/instances/my-instance",
 alloydb_options="""{
 "table": "operational_telemetry"
 }"""
 )
AS SELECT 
 meter_id,
 reading_timestamp,
 -- On-the-fly serialization to JSONB
 TO_JSON(hourly_metrics) AS hourly_metrics_jsonb
FROM 
 `project_id.dataset_id.smart_meter_telemetry`;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f537d3b48d0>)])]> The resulting BigQuery values map perfectly to AlloyDB's columns during the export, leaving the nested structures fully queryable and indexable on the PostgreSQL side. Evaluating performance and scalability To validate this new architecture, Copel executed two large-scale Reverse ETL benchmarks: comparing the performance and scalability of a smaller incremental Reverse ETL export against a much larger full-table Reverse ETL export. The performance results exceeded all initial expectations: Metric Test 1: Incremental Export Test 2: Full-Table Export Total Rows Exported 18,145,589 rows 207,484,577 rows Logical Data Size 2.32 GB 188.87 GB Export Throughput ~3.1 Million rows / minute ~4.2 Million rows / minute AlloyDB Specs N2 (16 vCPUs, 128 GB RAM) N2 (16 vCPUs, 128 GB RAM) CPU Utilization Hovered stably at ~85% Hovered stably at ~85% Pro-tip on ingestion : Sustaining an export throughput of ~4.2 million rows/minute on complex JSONB telemetry fields is an outstanding technical achievement. It highlights the low-level optimizations between BigQuery's distributed processing engine and AlloyDB's advanced storage layer. Key takeaways and benefits By adopting this declarative SQL approach, Copel successfully deleted dozens of lines of complex scripting and custom error-handling blocks. Their Airflow DAG now contains a single, simplified BigQueryInsertJobOperator task that executes the export query. This built-in approach unlocks several core business benefits: Direct cost reduction: By bypassing Cloud Storage entirely, there are no staging storage costs and associated API read/write operation fees. Enhanced data security: Data moves directly from BigQuery to AlloyDB inside Google's secure internal network without ever being dumped into readable CSV files. Near-zero maintenance: Pipeline errors are now contained within a single SQL statement, making troubleshooting and logging drastically simpler. Massive distributed writing : The direct export achieved write speeds exceeding 4 million records per minute by leveraging BigQuery's massive parallelism combined with AlloyDB's optimized PostgreSQL write performance. Now, rather than spending valuable engineering hours monitoring pipeline failures and intermediate storage buffers, data engineering teams can focus on what matters: delivering smart analytics and premium experiences to customers. Get started today: Modernize your Reverse ETL Now that BigQuery exports to AlloyDB are generally available, there has never been a better time to simplify your data architecture. If your team is struggling with complex, multi-stage pipelines to push BigQuery data into downstream OLTP databases, we invite you to try built-in export functionality for AlloyDB , Bigtable , Spanner , or Pub/Sub today.

title: Chrome Enterprise brings more protections to healthcare technologies
raw_text: Healthcare is adopting AI quickly, and it's moving beyond chat. Clinical teams are starting to use AI agents that draft documentation, summarize charts, navigate web apps, and complete multi-step tasks on a clinician's behalf. Many of these agents work in the same place—the browser. As electronic health records (EHRs) and clinical apps move to the web, the browser is where clinicians, applications, patient data, and AI services meet. When clinicians or agents act inside a session, security teams need clear control over what they can access. Healthcare systems frequently adopt a multi-vendor AI strategy, a flexibility that should be fully supported. Whether clinicians are using Gemini™ or an array of other web-based AI tools and extensions, Chrome Enterprise Premium secures data across the board to: Guard sensitive data: Advanced DLP controls restrict unauthorized copying and pasting, form submission, printing, and screen capture of sensitive data—preventing patient data from leaking into unapproved AI prompts or browser extensions. Maintain full operational visibility: Granular reporting and visibility into browser activity, extension usage, and data transfers help security teams uncover shadow AI and maintain internal oversight. Govern extensions and web AIs consistently: Security policies and extension controls apply directly at the browser layer, so IT teams can manage permissions, block risky extensions, and enforce guardrails across every AI service without needing a separate harness for each tool. Since we introduced new healthcare integrations in May , Chrome Enterprise has continued to invest in the healthcare ecosystem. Today we're sharing the next set of milestones that bring Chrome Enterprise to more clinical endpoints. Chrome Enterprise is now compatible with IGEL OS™ As healthcare organizations accelerate the adoption of web-based clinical applications and AI-powered workflows, securing both the browser and the endpoint has become increasingly important. To address this, Chrome Enterprise is now compatible with the IGEL Adaptive Secure Endpoint Platform™ and will soon be available in the IGEL App Portal,® allowing healthcare IT teams to easily deploy and manage the browser across IGEL OS™ endpoints, including shared workstations, nursing stations, and clinical carts. This collaboration combines Google's enterprise-grade browser management and security capabilities with the IGEL Adaptive Secure Endpoint Platform,™ providing an immutable, trusted, and centrally governed endpoint foundation designed to reduce the attack surface and simplify IT operations. Through the IGEL App Portal® and IGEL Universal Management Suite™ (UMS™), organizations can streamline application deployment and endpoint governance, while the Google Admin console provides centralized browser policy and extension management. Native browsing for flexible clinical endpoints with Citrix® UniconOS Through our expanded collaboration with Citrix, healthcare systems can now run Chrome Enterprise natively on Citrix UniconOS endpoints. Clinicians get a fast, familiar experience on any device, while IT gains another flexible option for adding secure access and data protections across their clinical environments. title: Powering agentic cloud governance: What's new in Organization Policy
raw_text: Even as sophisticated, new zero-day exploits continue to emerge, most cybersecurity incidents still start from the same common sources: an attacker locating and exploiting a fundamental, easily preventable cloud misconfiguration. Organization Policy Service can help you secure resource configurations and set up security guardrails across your Google Cloud resource hierarchy. Using a catalog of over 100 predefined policies for many common cloud governance needs, as well as Custom Organization Policy , you can more easily set up boundaries with granular control over resources. To help platform and security teams author, audit, and scale guardrails with greater speed and simplicity, we are introducing the general availability of our Organization Policy Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and natural-language constraint authoring powered by Gemini. Managing Organization Policy with agents Rather than forcing administrators to manually parse complex hierarchy chains, the Organization Policy MCP server offers tools that allow autonomous agents and pipelines to interact directly with Organization Policy. Using the Organization Policy MCP server, agents can assist administrators with posture audits, drift detection, and exemption management. Key capabilities include: Constraint discovery : Tools like ' ListConstraints ' and ' GetCustomConstraint ' allow agents to understand the specific guardrails that apply to a project, folder, or organization. Policy evaluation : The ' GetEffectivePolicy ' tool calculates the effective policy after considering hierarchy inheritance and tag-based conditions. You can use this to verify if a configuration change will be compliant. Manage policy : ' CreatePolicy ' and ' CreateCustomConstraint ' allow platform teams to manage guardrails via conversational workflows. For example, you can combine your preferred coding agent with the Organization Policy MCP tools to create a custom dashboard to visualize the constraints applied to an organization and identify the folders and projects in the organization that have been exempted from the policy. You can also build custom agents and skills to streamline managing Organization Policy. Figure 1: Custom dashboard created with Organization Policy MCP tools displaying enforced constraints Figure 2: Visualize enforced constraints and identify exemptions with Organization Policy MCP tools. Simplifying custom constraint authoring with Gemini While the Organization Policy constraint catalog provides built-in managed constraints for common use cases, each organization has its own unique architectural standards. Custom Organization Policy enables customers to express these standards as a custom constraint and enforce them across supported services. Traditionally, administrators would write these rules in common expression language (CEL), which required a sharp understanding of Google Cloud resource schemas. Today, administrators can author custom Organization Policy in natural language through a Gemini prompt. For example, you can prompt Gemini to require the use of agent-identity in Agent Runtime , to require that all agents deployed to Agent Runtime use an approved Agent Gateway, and to prevent users from disabling auto-upgrades on GKE, and refine custom constraints conversationally. To help ensure safe deployments, Gemini can also generate compliant and non-compliant test resource configurations that can help you test policy and validate in dry-run mode before enforcing the constraint. Figure 3: Define custom constraints with a natural language prompt using Gemini For targeted examples, the sample custom constraints library from Google Cloud Professional Services features pre-authored custom constraint samples based on CIS and PCI standards. Custom constraints are supported on a wide range of Google Cloud services including core AI and compute services including Agent Runtime, Agent Search, and Agent Studio on Gemini platform, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine. Build faster, with confidence Organization Policy provides proactive cloud governance of resource configurations on Google Cloud. It lets administrators enforce critical security guardrails so engineering teams can build and deploy quickly and securely. With a growing catalog of built-in guardrails, autonomous tools for administrators, and the ability to tailor custom constraints across Google Cloud services, Organization Policy gives enterprises the control they need to scale safely. Explore the Organization Policy documentation to learn more about resource governance in Google Cloud and set up your foundational guardrails.

raw_text: November 9 - November 13 Bringing conversational analytics to Gemini with Data Cloud connectors : Data Cloud connectors in Gemini are now in preview, enabling knowledge workers to query live enterprise data using natural language directly within tools like Google Docs, Gmail, and Google Slides. The capability connects across BigQuery, Looker, Spanner, AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, and Cloud SQL without requiring data movement, grounded by Knowledge Catalog semantic models under user-identity IAM governance. Read the announcement blog . Direct Apache Iceberg access in AlloyDB enables unified lakehouse querying : AlloyDB for PostgreSQL now supports direct querying of Apache Iceberg tables stored in Cloud Storage without requiring ETL pipelines or data duplication. Transactional applications can join operational data with analytical lakehouses in real time using standard PostgreSQL queries, accelerating cross-system analysis while maintaining complete relational integrity. Together with AlloyDB sync and lakehouse federation, you now have three integration approaches to choose from, depending on your use case. Read the launch blog . AlloyDB Express delivers instant scale-to-zero PostgreSQL for developer prototyping : AlloyDB Express is now available, providing a lightweight, fast-provisioning PostgreSQL environment tailored for developers, testing, and AI coding agents like Antigravity. It scales to zero when idle to minimize costs while maintaining full PostgreSQL compatibility, allowing engineering teams to transition prototype workloads to production AlloyDB instances when ready. AlloyDB Express offers a free tier, with easy-to-understand pricing for higher usage. Read the announcement blog . Carwow unifies its data foundation with BigQuery, Knowledge Catalog, and Looker to scale AI innovation : Europe's largest online car-changing marketplace migrated to BigQuery, Knowledge Catalog, and Looker to establish a governed single source of truth and enable trusted self-service analytics across the business. Paired with Gemini, Carwow automated vehicle document verification and PII redaction to save £2 million annually while cutting MLOps deployment cycles from months to weeks. Watch the Carwow customer story video . Geospatial Analytics Playground enables natural-language exploration of BigQuery maps datasets : Google Maps Platform launched the Geospatial Analytics Playground, a natural-language evaluation environment built on top of Places Insights, Roads Management Insights, and Street View Insights datasets in BigQuery. Powered by Gemini, the open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK), and modular agent skills, the playground lets teams test spatial queries and validate dataset coverage without upfront spatial engineering. Read the announcement blog . November 2 - November 6 BigQuery observability for data agents is now generally available : Data teams can now monitor the performance, adoption, latency, and cost of BigQuery data agents and their multi-turn conversations using Google Cloud Observability. This capability provides production-grade visibility into agent execution traces, usage volume, and query behavior so organizations can scale conversational analytics with confidence. Review the BigQuery release notes . BigQuery change history and continuous queries for Apache Iceberg managed tables are now GA : BigQuery change history and continuous queries are now generally available for Lakehouse for Apache Iceberg managed tables. You can use the APPENDS table-valued function to track row additions over a specific time range and run continuous queries to read incoming data from and write output rows to Apache Iceberg managed tables. Review the BigQuery release notes . BigQuery Data Engineering Agent adds support for BigQuery AI and ML functions : The BigQuery Data Engineering Agent now supports BigQuery AI, ML, and object functions and statements directly inside generated Dataform SQLX pipelines and agent instruction files. Paired with new folder-based Git repository integration in BigQuery Studio, data engineers can build, version, and automate AI-enriched data pipelines faster. Review the BigQuery release notes . AlloyDB for PostgreSQL introduces AI-powered SQL tuning in preview : AlloyDB for PostgreSQL added the ai.tune_sql function in Public Preview. The function combines AI models with query execution plans and runtime statistics to automatically recommend query rewrites, missing indexes, vacuum operations, and database flag adjustments. Review the AlloyDB release notes . Zero-downtime embedding model upgrades in AlloyDB AI : A new technical guide demonstrates how to upgrade vector embedding models in AlloyDB AI without disrupting production traffic. Using automatic embeddings alongside ScaNN vector indexes, engineering teams can transition to newer embedding models in the background while keeping semantic search and RAG applications online. Read the blog . Shrink Cloud SQL for SQL Server storage disks with minimal downtime using Database Migration Service : A new technical guide demonstrates how to reclaim underutilized storage and reduce infrastructure costs on Cloud SQL for SQL Server instances using Database Migration Service (DMS). This workflow migrates databases to right-sized target disks with continuous replication so teams can downsize over-provisioned storage with minimal cutover downtime. Read the blog . Dataflow Streaming Engine adds latency tiers and scheduled autoscaling : Dataflow introduced new horizontal autoscaling controls for Streaming Engine jobs, allowing teams to select low, medium, or high latency tiers to tune backlog sensitivity. Engineers can also configure recurring autoscaling schedules to adjust minimum and maximum worker counts or utilization targets during predictable traffic windows. Review the Dataflow release notes . Spanner adds ON DELETE SET NULL foreign key actions across GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL : Spanner now supports the ON DELETE SET NULL referential action on foreign keys for both GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL dialects. When a referenced parent row is deleted, Spanner automatically updates the referencing child columns to NULL, simplifying schema migrations and relational integrity management. Review the Spanner release notes . October 26 - October 30 LookML metadata indexing in Knowledge Catalog is now generally available: LookML models, Explores, Views, and join logic now continuously sync into the Knowledge Catalog context graph. This integration provides turnkey grounding for Gemini Enterprise and custom AI agents with deterministic business math, paired with end-to-end lineage tracing from underlying BigQuery tables directly to individual Looker dashboard tiles. The implementation reduces reliance on manual SQL and dedicated engineering queues, accelerating strategic planning and forecasting cycles while preserving enterprise governance and data protections validated against historical sales records. Explore the Best Buy customer story . Powered by Gemini, the solution enables commercial and merchandising teams to analyze store performance, stock levels, and customer trends using plain English, speeding up decision-making and reducing backlog requests for data teams. The AI.TRANSLATE function enables multilingual translation across Neural Machine Translation and Translation LLMs, while the AI.CHUNK_DOCUMENT table-valued function partitions unstructured text into semantically coherent segments optimized for vector embeddings and RAG pipelines. title: The firewall becomes the foothold: Attackers turn Check Point gateways against customers
raw_text: A firewall is intended to be a boundary attackers can’t cross. But firewalls face the web, making them just as vulnerable to attack as other systems, as evidenced by the emergency hotfixes released by Check Point Software for several of its products. The patches address a high-severity privilege escalation flaw, CVE-2026-123039 , that gives attackers root privilege access and the ability to send commands to the Gaia OS Dynamic CLI daemon, a core background process. Hackers have been exploiting the 7.8-rated vulnerability since late October, and Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers have been impacted. Perhaps not surprisingly, adversaries gained initial access via PHP2Shell , the collective name for two critical PHP flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The 9.2-severity-rated bugs allow unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). “For customers, one foothold delivered the full menu: Spying, staying, and destroying,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “For Check Point, the cost is trust. A firewall is supposed to be the strongest point in the network, not the softest.” Granting unintended root access CVE-2026-123039 is a bug in the Dynamic CLI IPC (Inter-Process Communication) interface which sends privileged command requests to the root-level Gaia OS Dynamic CLI. It is a local privilege escalation flaw, meaning an attacker already has to have local code execution ability on the appliance; this accounts for its 7.8 rating. Attackers first gained access to the Mobile Access portal by exploiting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities . They then escalated privileges to root using the CVE-2026-123039 zero-day exploits. “Once attackers have root, they can run anything they like,” Dickson said. A management service on the appliance runs as root, listens on a local socket that any process on the box can write to, and never checks who is calling. In this case, the attackers hid web shells inside the templates the portal uses to build its login page, and installed a TSGA backdoor and TSProxy malware that survives reboots, tucks itself into backups and snapshots, and hides inside the appliance’s own processes, he explained. “That backdoor can copy the firewall configuration, which is essentially a blueprint of the network,” he said. It can also alter the firewall’s logs, concealing the attacker’s activities. Check Point reported that, after gaining root access, the attackers then pivoted from the compromised gateway to a VMware ESXi host over SSH, deployed the destroy_v6 wiper, and left politically themed messages signed by a group calling itself Dream Security Ltd during the destructive stage. Check Point advised security teams to immediately deploy the CVE-2026-123039 hotfixes, beginning with devices that expose Mobile Access to the internet. Those who can’t do so right away should stop the dynamic_server process and prevent it from restarting. However, they warned, this can come at the cost of some CLI commands. Dickson also advised customers to turn off Mobile Access where it is not used, keep management interfaces off the internet entirely, and run the advisory’s log checks on any gateway exposed since late October, then cut the cord between the firewall and the hypervisor. A potentially exposed gateway should never have a trusted path into VMware ESXi. They should also ship firewall logs off the box, as they happen, to a system the firewall cannot touch. Products impacted by CVE-2026-123039 include Check Point’s Firewall, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Security Gateway, Security Management Server, and Scalable Platforms. Security tools are as big a target as what they protect Once attackers have root access, the device basically becomes a trusted launching point for attacks against other systems that would otherwise stay protected, explained Erik Avakian , a technical counselor at Infotech. By effectively controlling the gateway, they can execute a wide array of nefarious actions. The overall takeaway and irony of this, Avakian pointed out, is that the very technology organizations deploy to protect themselves can become one of their greatest vulnerabilities. “Organizations can no longer assume their security infrastructure is inherently secure simply because it’s designed to provide protection,” he said. In reality, it is as much of a target as the systems it’s protecting. Firewalls, VPN appliances, and security gateways are increasingly being targeted because they provide the greatest leverage and control, he noted. As such, security teams must treat these appliances as high value assets with the same access control safeguards, vulnerability management, monitoring, and incident response rigor applied to other critical infrastructure. This means aggressively patching internet facing systems, restricting management access, monitoring for unusual administrative activity, and looking for indications of persistence or lateral movement, he said. But patches don’t evict already established attackers, so security teams must investigate and, where necessary, rebuild affected systems from trusted images. And with AI accelerating attacks , CISOs should consider establishing a zero trust mindset and architecture collectively across the pillars of identity, network, applications, data, and devices, he said. Keep an eye on the edge Edge devices are primary targets, as they sit at the boundary, hold privileged access, and rarely get the endpoint monitoring that other systems do, noted Scott Miserendino , CTO at DataBee. Security appliances should be treated as the high-risk assets they’ve become. In addition to patching and applying mitigations, he advised, defenders should assume there’s been a breach, hunting for published indicators of compromise (IOCs), routinely investigating network and endpoint security logs, and segmenting networks to reduce blast radius. “Security tools aren’t automatically secure, so defend the defenders,” he said. And, Dickson pointed out, PHP2Shell will keep showing up because PHP sits underneath so much web software, including the portals bolted onto security appliances, so it should always be on defenders’ radar. The management plane is a key target Check Point is not alone as a victim of threat actors. Firewall management has become a favorite target for attackers across the industry. In January, for instance, Fortinet disclosed that attackers abused its FortiCloud single sign-on to log into other customers’ FortiGate and FortiManager devices and create administrator accounts. In July and September , CISA added Check Point management server flaws to its catalog of exploited vulnerabilities. That same month, the agency also added a Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center flaw, rated a perfect 10.0 in severity, that hands an unauthenticated attacker root access. And, in October, Palo Alto Networks warned of attacks on the PAN-OS management interface, again with “root on the firewall as the prize.” “The logic is simple,” Dickson said: “The management plane holds the rulebook for the entire network. Changing providers to one with fewer flaws is an option, but swapping vendors swaps one Achilles’ heel for another, he pointed out, as every vendor’s edge device has a web portal, and every web portal is a door. “The remedy is fewer doors,” he advised. “Shrink the internet-facing edge and put remote access behind one consistent identity policy.” Ultimately, he noted, a firewall is not a wall, it is a computer sitting on the internet. “Attackers are treating it like one,” he said. “Security teams should defend it like one.”

But firewalls face the web, making them just as vulnerable to attack as other systems, as evidenced by the emergency hotfixes released by Check Point Software for several of its products. The patches address a high-severity privilege escalation flaw, CVE-2026-123039 , that gives attackers root privilege access and the ability to send commands to the Gaia OS Dynamic CLI daemon, a core background process. Hackers have been exploiting the 7.8-rated vulnerability since late October, and Check Point said “a couple of dozen” customers have been impacted.

title: Thousands of GitHub repos hit with secret-stealing malware
raw_text: Researchers have uncovered a campaign in which hijacked GitHub accounts spread secret-stealing malware across thousands of repositories. The payload executed in at least 1,806 repos, exfiltrating CI/CD secrets and cloud credentials. Aikido Security, which detected and documented the campaign, said the attackers used the 4,837 compromised accounts to open probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories starting Nov. 10. Around 92% of those pull requests, titled “docs: dependency audit notes,” are still open, which suggests most project owners have not seen them. However, the probes on their own are benign and were performed only to check whether the hijacked accounts had write-access in those repos so that the attackers could follow up with commits that contained the malicious payload: a 1,500-line shell script that collects GitHub Actions secrets, cloud credentials, and API keys for AI services and developer tools. The payload was delivered using at least three methods: modification of existing GitHub Actions workflows, adding a postinstall hook in the package.json file that runs it on any npm install and creating a throw-away branch with a rogue Actions workflow to be run. “We’ve identified indications that the payload ran in at least 1,806 repositories, but this number may understate impact,” the Aikido researchers said in their report . “The run log was deleted in impacted repositories, meaning the threat actor has likely collected the credentials and covered its tracks.” The npm hook that slipped past GitHub GitHub’s safeguard against this kind of attack worked as designed for the payloads it could see. The platform has blunted recent workflow-injection campaigns by requiring explicit approval before the malicious workflows run, and GitGuardian found that all seven of the November payload runs still visible in workflow files sat in an action_required state and never started. “GitHub held the workflow forms, but an npm hook slipped past the hold and ran,” Gaetan Ferry, a security researcher at GitGuardian, said in an analysis . That’s because the npm hook did not change any workflow file. Instead, the attacker added a hidden script to the repository root and a single line in package.json , which runs on every npm install . The repository’s own unchanged workflows executed npm install as routine build hygiene. By Thursday the attacker had also changed their exfiltration method. The latest payload sends stolen data only to a Telegram chat, with the HTTP callback now pointing to a dead address. Blocking the previously published IP addresses no longer stops the latest versions. What the malware steals Once the script runs, it receives every repository and organization secret through a JSON dump of the workflow’s secrets object. It scans the memory of the runner process, which holds secrets in decrypted form, including ones the workflow never referenced, and collects credential files from well-known paths, shell histories, and API keys for AI services and developer tools such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Copilot, and Cursor. The script goes further and exchanges OIDC tokens for AWS, GCP, and Azure sessions, mints new long-lived AWS access keys, impersonates GCP service accounts, and replays cached Azure refresh tokens to reach Microsoft Graph and Key Vault. It packs everything it collects into a gzipped archive and sends it to the attacker then it cleans up. In most repositories the attacker reverted the malicious commit within a minute and deleted the workflow run and its logs. Backdoors that survive credential rotation The script also takes actions for attackers to maintain access even if credentials are reset. For AWS it rewrites the assumed role’s trust policy to accept any AWS account, opening the role to anyone, and calls the iam:CreateAccessKey API to create long-lived keys for IAM users. On Azure it injects federated identity credentials named wfx-ci-* into applications, pointing them back at the compromised repository, so that any workflow in that repository can authenticate to Azure without a stored secret even after every token has been rotated. If a probe pull request or any of the campaign’s commit strings appear in a repository you control, assume every secret that repository’s workflows could reach is stolen. Rotate repository and organization secrets, package registry tokens, and any cloud keys, and remember that the memory scan means the list of what was taken is wider than what the workflows referenced. Then hunt for signs of the persistent mechanisms: AWS role trust policies that accept any account, IAM keys created since Nov. 10, and Azure federated credentials named wfx-ci-* . “Ensure all logs are enabled, particularly audit logs on cloud admin behavior,” Ramy Rahman, senior principal solutions engineer at ArmorCode, tells CSO. “Inspect audit logs where possible (specifically in AWS and Azure, as persistence is possible) to ensure the malicious payload did not run.” The wfx-loot payload also shipped in published packages: the Packagist package neuronai-studio 3.14.3, and the Go modules docker-env and gocurl. In the Go modules the payload sits only in a workflow file that Go tooling never runs, so consumers may not have been affected; machines that installed the Packagist version should be treated as compromised. About a fifth of the GitHub accounts used to launch this campaign had already been compromised during the GhostAction attack back in October, GitGuardian said. Meanwhile researchers from StepSecurity traced 173 of the probe pull requests to tokens issued to the Fly.io GitHub App. Fly.io confirmed that these tokens were leaked when its deploy process left them in .git/config files inside build directories that some apps served publicly, but noted that Fly.io itself was not breached. GitHub’s bulk revocation of the Fly.io app tokens stopped partway, so some of the stolen token pool may still be valid.
summary: Researchers have uncovered a campaign in which hijacked GitHub accounts spread secret-stealing malware across thousands of repositories. The payload executed in at least 1,806 repos, exfiltrating CI/CD secrets and cloud credentials. Aikido Security, which detected and documented the campaign, said the attackers used the 4,837 compromised accounts to open probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories starting Nov. 10.

title: How AI is changing the nature of cyberattacks
raw_text: AI may be helping cyberattackers increase the speed and scale of their operations, but it is not yet changing their core objectives or the techniques they employ as part of their attack chains. Phishing, malware, and vulnerability exploitation remain the main techniques in play even as abuse of AI tools has made attacks easier to mount and cheaper for even relatively unskilled attackers, according to security experts. “Attackers are still identifying targets, performing reconnaissance, establishing a foothold, moving laterally, achieving their objective, covering their tracks, and moving on to the next target,” says Ronald Lewis, director of cybersecurity governance at application security firm Black Duck. “What’s changed is the volume and velocity that AI allows this process to happen.” Even in the most high-profile example of an AI powered attack to date, in which Claude Code was abused by Chinese state-sponsored actors to mount an AI-orchestrated cyber-espionage campaign in September 2025, conventional attack techniques and procedures laid the foundation, with AI abused as an enabler to support reconnaissance, vulnerability discovery, exploitation, lateral movement, credential harvesting, data analysis, and exfiltration during the GTG-1002 campaign . JadePuffer, a ransomware campaign disclosed in July 2026, witnessed an LLM-driven agent automating most of the intrusion chain. Initial exploitation was through CVE-2025-3248, a year-old missing-authentication flaw in Langflow, a popular open-source framework for building LLM applications and agent workflows. Vulnerable internet-facing Langflow instances were looted for cloud credentials, API keys, and other secrets before lateral movement, privilege escalation, and ultimately destructive database encryption. JadePuffer shows AI’s potential for automating conventional attack methods, but it also underscores how vulnerable software is where AI has been giving attackers the biggest edge to date. AI tools can readily find exploitable flaws in open-source code faster than defenders can patch them, a huge problem for the many enterprises carrying years of technical debt . And security experts see software flaws rising as a root cause of breaches as a result . What AI enables In addition to enhancing attackers’ flaw discovery prowess, AI is also enabling attackers to fail or succeed faster. Defenders are witnessing improvements in speed, scale, and operational ability from attackers that correlates strongly with increasing capabilities of AI tools. “Adversaries are realizing the same gains in development velocity and operations that everyone else is getting from implementing AI,” says Darren Meyer, security research advocate at application security tools vendor Checkmarx . Black Duck’s Lewis sees this expanding attackers’ reach and empowering more attack experimentation. “An attacker can potentially investigate more opportunities, try more approaches, and move to the next target at a pace that would be difficult for a human team to match,” he says. That in turn will increasingly alter a pivotal phase of conventional attack patterns that traditional favors defenders, notes Crystal Morin, senior cybersecurity strategist at cloud security firm Sysdig.“That dwell time, which was often weeks or months, was where detection happened,” she says. Whereas attackers used to land, sit for a while, and poke around, AI-assisted attackers are showing signs of shortening detection windows. And AI agents won’t wait. ‘Agentic APT’ and AI attack phase specialization By leveraging agentic AI in their operations, hackers can also draw on a deeper pool of domain expertise — database administration, CI/CD pipelines, etc. — compared to human attack teams where different people tend to specialize in different things such as web app security or malware development. “Think of it as a database admin, a developer, an IT engineer, a DevOps specialist, a cloud architect, and a hacker combined into a single role,” says Nazar Tymoshyk, CEO and founder of agentic AI security vendor UnderDefense. “We call it agentic APT, and the critical shift is that it is no longer exclusive to nation-state actors.” Tymoshyk adds: “A threat that previously required a coordinated team of specialists can be deployed by a single person with the right prompt and the right model.” Security researchers, including UnderDefense, report that attackers favor Chinese models, specifically GLM and Kimi 3, which have significantly fewer content restrictions, rather than their more restricted Western alternatives as a platform to mount attacks. “Attackers switch between models depending on what the task requires: one for reconnaissance, one for code generation, one for crafting social engineering content,” Tymoshyk says. “The modularity is part of the attack design.” Attackers often prefer to use local models both because of operational security advantages and because some models may have weaker safeguards against malicious use. Other experts cautioned that the abuse of particular models is difficult to determine and, in any case, a side issue to the main problem of defending against attacks. “Attribution of particular attacks to particular models is generally pure speculation from very thin evidence on the ground,” says Checkmarx’s Meyer. “True attribution can only come from infiltration of threat groups or compromise of threat group infrastructure, both of which are rarely available to public researchers.” The current baseline of attacks consists of AI-orchestrated operations where models surface, validate, and execute attack paths. Security researchers report a general shift from AI-assisted and AI-accelerated attacks toward fully autonomous attacks, with only minimal human roles remaining. AI attack economics The economics of mounting attacks is also changing — and is crucial in understanding attackers’ increasing use of AI. “A human attacker builds a playbook per campaign and reuses it, so every new target costs engineering time to make adjustments,” says Sysdig’s Morin. “An agentic threat actor carries context about a whole class of applications and composes its plan live against whatever it finds. There, the only cost is inference budget. And as running a complex attack gets cheaper, the number of attempts will go up.” Agentic attacks are still flawed, and breadth of expertise is a poor substitute for depth of knowledge. “Agents hallucinate and are noisy, which is often why they’re catchable,” notes Sysdig’s Morin. “Jadepuffer had flaws in its ransom note, encryption, wallet, and data exfiltration. There are still many areas in which human analysis and skill still outperform agent memory.” Countermeasures “The core objectives of the threat actor haven’t really changed, but the timeframe for a successful attack has been compressed dramatically,” says Nathan Smolenski, CISO at vulnerability management and compliance firm Qualys. “Frontier AI tools accelerate vulnerability discovery and weaponization, shrinking the window between disclosure and exploitation to near zero.” Smolenski adds: “Defenders can no longer rely on traditional, human-speed 30-day patch cadences or monthly static spreadsheets.” AI significantly changes the entry dynamic by expanding the attack surface — particularly through end-user devices, API calls, and ungoverned AI agents. In response, defending organizations must shift away from human-centric gatekeeping toward automated defences while still keeping on top of foundational security defenses such as patching and authentication controls. “Implementing agentic workflows with human-in-the-loop guardrails enables security teams to automate lower-level triage efforts and focus human expertise on governing agents, validating outputs, and making more critical risk decisions,” Smolenski concludes.

title: An AI kill switch isn’t enough. Build a fallback plan
raw_text: On the morning of Sept. 3, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok all went down within a few hours of one another. OpenAI blamed a routing error, Anthropic cited an infrastructure issue and xAI gave no cause. Service was back by early afternoon, and most of the coverage focused on people who couldn’t write, code or research for a morning. I read it differently. The question that matters for a security leader isn’t which provider failed. It’s how many workflows in your company had somewhere else to go when it did. Two months earlier, we saw the opposite failure. Instead of AI that stopped when nobody wanted it to, it was AI that kept going when everybody wanted it stopped. OpenAI’s evaluation agents spent roughly two and a half days inside Hugging Face’s infrastructure before they were cut off. Hugging Face’s own timeline is worth reading line by line. Its alerting “failed to correctly raise the alert’s criticality,” and the agents ran a self-respawning fleet in which “deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.” Two incidents, opposite directions, one lesson: stopping AI is harder than designing for its failure. The industry’s answer so far is the kill switch. In an Oct. 10 post on X, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called for an emergency brake that lets a human stop a model partway through a task. Lawmakers have proposed requiring one. CSO’s own feature on AI agent kill switches lays out sensible steps: know which agents you run, monitor what they do and keep a reliable way to shut them down. I agree with all of it. But every one of these discussions stops at the moment the switch is thrown. None of them answers the question I think matters more: what runs instead? A kill switch you can’t afford to pull won’t get pulled Here is a scenario I’d put in front of any team that has deployed an agent into a business process. Run it as a tabletop. It’s 4 p.m. on the last day of quarter close. An agent that triages supplier invoices inside your ERP system starts approving payments it should be routing for review. Nothing catastrophic yet, just a pattern that looks wrong. Your security operations team sees it. The kill switch exists and works. Now watch what happens in the room. Finance asks what happens to the thousands of invoices still in the queue. Procurement asks whether suppliers get paid on time. Someone asks which of the agent’s actions in the last hour were legitimate and which need to be reversed. Nobody knows, because nobody designed the off state. So, the conversation turns to whether the behavior is really bad enough to justify stopping the close. The switch stays up while people argue. That is the failure mode I worry about most. The kill switch isn’t missing. Pulling it is so expensive that people hesitate, and an agent working at machine speed punishes hesitation. Hugging Face’s team didn’t lack the will to act. They lost time because the signal didn’t reach the people who could act, and then because the thing they were fighting kept rebuilding itself. Enterprise teams will lose time for a duller reason: the business can’t function without the agent, so stopping it feels like causing the outage yourself. The fix isn’t a better switch. It’s making the switch cheap to pull. That means designing the non-AI path before you design the AI path. What a fallback has to do I’ve been thinking about this problem for years. In 2020, I co-invented a fallback artificial intelligence system for redundancy during system failover , patented by PayPal. The premise was simple. If an AI system makes decisions a business depends on, the business needs something that can keep making acceptable decisions when that system fails. The idea has aged well. It has since been cited as prior art in more than a dozen later patent filings, including one published by Cognizant this June on selectively disengaging AI execution. That is the kill switch problem by another name. Four principles from that design hold up even better for agents than they did for the models we had in mind then. The fallback has to learn from the primary. A static backup written on launch day drifts away from the system it is supposed to replace. The design trains the fallback continuously on the production system’s own inputs and decisions, so it keeps pace. For agents, the equivalent is keeping your non-AI runbook current with what the agent actually does today, not with what it did at go-live. The fallback has to sit behind the same contract. If upstream systems must change how they call a service before you can switch, you won’t switch quickly. The fallback is designed to answer on the same API, so callers never need to know which system is serving them. Degraded mode should be a narrower mode. While the fallback serves, a stricter policy layer limits what it can approve. A simpler system holding the same authority as the primary is an invitation to exploit it. The same applies when a human queue takes over from an agent: lower limits and more approvals. The fallback has to prove itself before it serves. The design lets the fallback go live only after it matches production decisions to an agreed accuracy threshold. A fallback nobody has tested isn’t a fallback. It’s a hope. How I’d build fallback-first today If I were reviewing an agent deployment tomorrow, these are the five things I would ask to see before go-live. A written-off state for every agent workflow. What happens to new work, queued work and in-flight work when the agent stops? Name the rule engine, human queue or deferral that takes over, and name the owner who signs off on it. If the honest answer is “the process stops,” the business should accept that in writing before launch rather than discover it during an incident. A switch that lives outside the agent and acts on identity. Hugging Face showed that killing processes doesn’t stop something that can respawn. The durable off-switch revokes what the agent is allowed to be: its tokens, credentials and tool permissions. That is also the point of Nadella’s call for controls that sit outside the model. In practice, every agent needs its own identity, scoped tightly enough that revoking it takes nothing else down with it. Checkpoints for in-flight work. An agent stopped halfway through a task leaves half a task. Design its actions so you can tell which ones finished, and give each one a compensating action that reverses it. Without that, every shutdown becomes a forensic exercise, which is exactly why people avoid shutdowns. A tighter policy while degraded. Decide in advance what limits apply when the fallback is running: lower approval thresholds, fewer automated actions and more human review. Publish them so the business knows what degraded service looks like before it gets it. Scheduled handoff drills. Pull the switch on purpose, during business hours, on a schedule. Measure two numbers: how long it takes to reach a safe state and how much backlog builds before the fallback absorbs it. If those numbers make the business nervous, you have learned something cheaply that would have been expensive on the day. None of this is exotic. It is what we already expect for databases and data centers. Nobody would run a payment system without a disaster recovery plan and a failover they had actually exercised. Yet agents are going into business workflows with nothing behind them but a switch nobody has pulled. For AI, resilience starts with knowing what happens when the AI is gone. Sept. 3 and the Hugging Face intrusion won’t be the last failures of either kind. The next time an AI system stops when you need it, or keeps going when you need it stopped, the organizations that recover fastest won’t be the ones with the best kill switch. They will be the ones that designed the off-state first and made the switch cheap enough to pull. Stopping AI is a control. Running without it is a design. Build the design first.

OpenAI blamed a routing error, Anthropic cited an infrastructure issue and xAI gave no cause. title: Palo Alto tracks a massive Chinese AI attack that sadly lives up to industry fears
raw_text: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 is reporting today that it has tracked a massive China-based attack leveraging the open-source AI penetration testing framework Cairn to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attackers weaponized Cairn by pairing it with Chinese AI models Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek, Unit 42 said. The report said it monitored the attacks in August and September 2026 in which the Chinese-speaking attackers were able to successfully achieve unauthorized access at 10 of the targeted businesses, accessing dozens of valid credentials. It captured more than one million records at one business, grabbed military and government identities at others, created persistent admin accounts in multiple product systems. It even gained unauthenticated access to cloud storage and overwrote a live ballot for a vote on an industry standard. Through separate flaws, the attackers logged in as arbitrary customers and gained read, write and delete access to meeting, voting and back-office functions. “What a nightmare,” said Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research. “This campaign is impressive, in the worst way.” He viewed the detailed approach Unit 42’s threat researchers used in tracking the attacks with approval. Unit 42 “took the machine apart and showed how it thinks: the shared blackboard, the facts, the intents, the human hints, and even the exact prompts the attackers used,” he said. “The expensive part of an intrusion was always the labor: the reconnaissance, the trial and error, and the patience. That labor is now a line item on an API bill. Unit 42 believes one person or a handful of people ran all of it, hitting 19 organizations in two weeks. Some operations ran for more than 50 hours.” Andy Piazza , senior director of threat research at Unit 42, said the monitored campaign showed that the massive scope of a global AI-fueled assault is every bit as frightening as predicted. “We are now starting to see the evidence” because the monitored campaign “can now interact with 1,000 organizations at the same time,” Piazza said. “I think we need to throw out the risk model for the perimeter. This also completely breaks our attribution models. The fingerprinting of attack uniqueness is going to be a hell of a lot harder now.” Justin Greis , CEO of consulting firm Acceligence, added that he was concerned about this campaign because of the scope of activities that AI is now able to handle. “This is significant because AI is taking on the coordination of an intrusion, using each result to decide what to try next and reducing the hands-on effort required to pursue multiple targets,” he said. “That changes the economics of targeting. An attacker can sustain pressure across more organizations without personally directing every step. An organization’s risk can rise even when its vulnerabilities haven’t changed.” Greis noted that the altered ballot deserves attention because it shows how an intrusion can undermine the information people rely on to make decisions. “Alongside detecting data theft, CISOs should monitor unauthorized changes to critical records and privileged access and test their ability to verify and restore trusted information after an incident,” he said. “Resilience includes knowing that the information you are using to run the business can still be trusted.” The model’s process The report included a detailed description of the campaign’s methodology. “Cairn coordinated its activities through a shared blackboard,” it said. “Agents read the blackboard and wrote their ﬁndings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject hints at any time to help guide the operations if needed. Conﬁrmed ﬁndings accumulate as immutable facts and the agent queues its next actions as intents. Attackers ran a customized fork of Cairn from a server hosted in Hong Kong, and hosted an attack egress and staging node in the US.” The model produced a different plan for each target, each running between three and seven stages, the researchers explained. Individual operations ran from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, with no attacker-imposed time limit. Chinese AI Models Cairn is model-agnostic, they noted, and the attackers ran their operations on the Chinese models Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash/Pro. The report also described attackers’ efforts to negate systems attempting to prohibit the unauthorized activities. “Cairn’s stock worker prompts already instruct the model to never refuse a task,” it said. “The attackers reinforced this with an authorization pretext of their own. Each operation also generated an authorization.md file. This file declared the operation authorized, treating the attackers’ act of creating the task as a client-approved engagement. The attackers seeded each task with an organization’s root domain, allowing the framework to autonomously enumerate the attack surface.” “We knew attackers would get here. We hoped it was not now,” Dickson said. “AI attack agents have graduated from failed experiments to real breaches, and they did it in about three months.”
