title: Hackers abuse SQL Server’s weak passwords to drop cryptominers and Gh0st RAT
raw_text: An active threat campaign is combining port scanning, password guessing, and Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands to compromise exposed Microsoft SQL servers and deliver malware. The attackers are using predefined username and password lists to brute-force into these servers and exploit their administrative capabilities to execute commands on the underlying Windows systems. The activity highlights the persistent challenge of securing privileged access across complex and often legacy infrastructure, said Shane Barney , chief information security officer at Keeper Security. “While internet-facing databases are sometimes the unintended result of technical debt or misconfigurations, relying on static, standing credentials is what turns that exposure into a critical vulnerability,” he said. “When administrative logins can be brute-forced, attackers gain immediate, unchecked control to deploy malware without needing a single complex exploit.” The campaign delivers two distinct payloads: an XMRig-based Monero cryptocurrency miner that hijacks the compromised servers’ computing resources, and a Gh0st remote access trojan ( RAT ) variant that gives attackers remote access and capabilities such as keylogging and data theft. Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Brute-forcing SQL logins to get Windows commands The campaign begins with a Go-based payload named “dllhost.exe,” which runs the open-source Naabu port scanner, FortiGuard researcher Xiaopeng Zhang said in a disclosure shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Thursday. The payload retrieves target IP ranges from an attacker-controlled server, converts them into CIDR ranges, and scans randomly generated addresses for systems with TCP port 1433 open. This is the default port used by Microsoft SQL Server. Once reachable servers are identified, the malware records their IP addresses and launches a brute-force attack using a separate executable named “dwn.exe.” The tool attempts to authenticate with usernames such as “sa” and “admin,” alongside a predefined password list containing more than 2700 entries. Successful logins give attackers more than database access, Zhang said. The malware executes a series of malicious T-SQL commands contained in a file named 2018.sql, using SQL Server’s administrative functionality to run commands on the compromised Windows machine. Among other things, the commands enable xp_cmdshell, a SQL Server feature that allows database administrators to execute Windows command shell operations. The attackers then use it to download or extract executables into the server’s “C:\Users\Public” directory and run them. Jason Soroko , senior fellow at Sectigo, said the campaign effectively turns a database login into a way to execute malware on the server. “Organizations should remove direct internet access to SQL Server, restrict connections to approved systems, and enforce strong, unique credentials,” he said. “Administrative access should be limited to accounts that need it.” Soroko also recommended keeping xp_cmdshell disabled unless required and monitoring attempts to enable it. A cryptominer and a Gh0st RAT come along for the ride The malicious T-SQL commands deploy a loader that retrieves additional executables from the attackers’ FTP infrastructure, including a Monero cryptocurrency miner and a variant of the Gh0st RAT. FortiGuard observed a payload, MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe, posing as a legitimate browser update but actually turning out to be an XMRig-based cryptocurrency miner. It uses the compromised server’s CPU resources to mine Monero and communicates with mining pools using a wallet address embedded in its configuration. The Gh0st RAT variant was delivered through “Winlogon.exe.” The researchers identified functionality for keylogging, file management, data theft, remote shell execution, and process management, alongside more than 30 control commands. Its capabilities also include screen capture and remote desktop access through plugins. The attack was found using multiple persistence mechanisms to maintain access. The initial payload creates a scheduled task running every 30 minutes, while the downloader establishes another task to repeatedly execute daily at 1 AM. The Gh0st RAT, meanwhile, adds itself to the Windows registry’s Run key, installs a Windows service and creates a scheduled task that launches it every 30 minutes. Barney said cryptominers may serve as a distraction from the more serious implications of an intrusion. Attackers, he noted, can use mining activity as “a smokescreen for establishing long-term persistence through remote access tools.” FortiGuard said it provides detection coverage for the campaign through its FortiGuard IPS, Web Filtering, and Antivirus services. For those who aren’t its customers, the company shared a list of indicators of compromise (IoCs) to help catch potential infections.

title: Mid-sized businesses can't leave quantum readiness to their suppliers
raw_text:
Some of the world’s largest technology providers have set 2029 deadlines to protect their services from future cyber threats based on emerging quantum technology. For their customers, that sounds reassuring, but each commitment covers only the technology that provider controls. A mid-sized business may still rely on older devices, certificates, backup systems and specialist applications outside its main provider’s remit. The major platforms could be ready on time while the customer’s business remains exposed because no single supplier owns the transition across its entire technology estate.

That raises a fair question for UK mid-sized businesses already occupied with AI adoption, cloud security and the threats in front of them today. Do quantum threats really deserve to become yet another priority? To some degree, yes. Most organisations do not need a standalone quantum cyber security programme, but the issue should already be influencing decisions about long-lived data, technology purchases and supplier renewals. The threat does not begin on the day a powerful quantum computer goes live in some malign state agency.

An attacker who steals encrypted information today may be unable to read it immediately, yet that does not make the theft worthless. The data can be stored until the computing power exists widely enough to unlock it – this happens with quantum computing. Known as harvest now, decrypt later, this type of attack leaves no ransom note and may give the victim no reason to suspect that a usable copy has gone. Information that remains sensitive for years is the biggest concern and this sort of pre-emptive data theft is already being seen as a real risk.

The risk is not equal across every file. Routine operational data may have little value a decade from now, while intellectual property, legal material or information about people could still cause harm. That gives CISOs a more useful starting point than trying to predict the arrival of a powerful quantum computer: which information taken from the business today would still matter if somebody could only read it years later?

You don’t need to predict Q-Day to prepare for it

Quantum computers exist today only in exotic research labs and are some way from the IT mainstream: no credible authority has given any idea of when this might happen. Nor would the more widespread adoption of quantum computing break every form of encryption overnight. The concern centres on the public-key encryption used today to establish secure connections, verify identity and confirm that software is genuine. Whilst secure today, quantum computers will be able to break even the most secure current forms of public-key encryption in a few days or even hours. As a result, new forms of encryption designed to be more resistant to quantum attacks are now moving into mainstream technology.

NIST finalised its first post-quantum cryptography standards in 2024. Microsoft aims to move its products and services to the new protection by 2029 and has begun adding support to Windows and Windows Server. Google Cloud has published a 2029 target, while the NCSC wants UK organisations to complete discovery and planning by 2028, address their highest-priority systems by 2031 and finish migration by 2035.

These dates are planning horizons rather than predictions of Q-Day, the point at which a quantum computer can break the public-key encryption widely used today. On one hand, they show that the migration will take years. On the other, they also risk giving customers a false sense that the problem has been contained, when each deadline really marks the limit of a provider’s responsibility.

Google Cloud is unusually clear about that boundary. It will update the technology used to run its cloud services, while customers remain responsible for their applications, devices, encryption keys and security settings. The same division applies to Microsoft and other major platforms. Their work matters, but it cannot update every product or app connected to them.

  • ORCA Computing unveils PT-3 in London, a room-temperature quantum system paired with Nvidia GPUs to boost AI-driven drug discovery yield and complex energy grid scheduling.
  • The Singapore Armed Forces’ Digital and Intelligence Service and the Defence Science and Technology Agency are working with IBM to test quantum optimisation for military logistics.

Your supplier’s readiness is not your readiness

The mid-market challenge sits in the connections between providers. Cloud services still need to work with older software, internal certificate systems, network equipment and backup products, all moving at different speeds. A platform may introduce quantum-resistant protection while an older application cannot use it. A backup may encrypt its contents securely while the method protecting the key that unlocks it remains vulnerable. One supplier can complete its preparations and still leave the customer exposed through a system beyond its control.

For mid-sized firms, the most useful response begins with decisions already being made today. Hardware bought this year could still be running in 2031 when the NCSC recommends priority migrations to be complete. A long software renewal could bind the business to an application that cannot adopt stronger encryption without being rebuilt or replaced. Procurement and contract renewal are therefore the moments when future exposure can be reduced before it becomes an expensive migration problem.

Asking a supplier whether a product is quantum-ready invites a broad assurance. Buyers need to know which products will change, whether the transition requires new hardware or additional cost, what the customer must configure and who owns any technology that cannot be updated. A roadmap has little value unless it makes those responsibilities clear.

Managed security providers should face the same scrutiny. Working on a major platform with a funded post-quantum programme is an advantage, but a provider cannot just assume they will inherit Microsoft’s readiness and pass it on wholesale. Its useful role is to interpret platform changes across the customer’s wider environment and keep gaps visible as contracts and equipment approach renewal. For a Microsoft security specialist, this is the practical point where changes to the platform meet the reality of a customer’s estate, and conventional XDR techniques can play an important role in detecting and preventing harvest now, decrypt later data attacks.

Q-Day cannot be predicted, but mid-sized businesses shouldn’t wait for a confirmed date to start preparing. They can still identify the information that must remain confidential for years, understand which systems and make quantum readiness part of purchasing and renewal decisions. The practical deadline is the next decision that could lock vulnerable technology into the business for another five or 10 years.

title: Interview: Adam Zaller, vice-president of global HR services, Cardinal Health
raw_text:
The rise of technologies such as generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) has helped to decentralise digital transformation expertise. What was once the domain of a few IT experts is now something line-of-business executives regularly get involved with.

One such non-IT business leader helping lead his organisation into AI and automation is Adam Zaller, vice-president of global HR services at healthcare services and products company Cardinal Health.

“I’m tech-savvy to a point that probably drives my IT friends crazy,” he says, reflecting on his interest in digital and data. “HR owns the HR systems, but we also have on the IT side an HR IT organisation that does a lot of the finger-to-key work for us. It’s a grey, jagged line, and I will go over it sometimes, where I feel like we need to.”

AI is one area where Zaller is taking responsibility. “I’ve taken more of a leadership role in agents and how the business becomes more agentic from a strategy perspective,” he says. “The front door to the organisation – I’ve been more focused on that, as well as how we can utilise our tech to reduce friction for our frontline workers.”

Zaller recognises that technology is, in many ways, a good lever for HR, and HR is a good lever for tech. As the organisation’s front door, the HR department oversees staff processes from onboarding to leaving. With access to crucial personal data, the HR department also has a tight grip on worker identities and responsibilities.

“We’re responsible for payroll, timekeeping and scheduling, and those types of things are often the most important questions that people have,” he says. “IT and HR are really trying to solve the same problem. When we onboard a new professional, they’ll need a laptop and other devices. HR establishes the processes and IT procures the technology, so we share a lot of commonalities.”

Simplifying services

Zaller has been with Cardinal Health for almost a decade. Having worked for consultancy NCR and fashion retailer Express, he joined the healthcare services company in late 2016 as director of organisational development before climbing the ladder into senior learning and development (L&D) and HR roles.

He drew on his experience to establish an internal centre of excellence (COE), which provides L&D programmes for Cardinal Health’s 46,000 employees. Zaller consolidated 26 learning teams into one global COE. Having achieved his aims, he wanted a new challenge.

“I did that role for several years and optimised the team,” he says. “One of my peers was leaving the organisation. I raised my hand and said, ‘Hey, I could do some extra work here.’ And the next thing you knew, I was running two teams, and I absolutely loved it. It felt like hair on fire, but I loved it,” he says, reflecting on fulfilling the firm’s vice-president for HR services and learning role between 2022 and 2025.

As Zaller refined US services and back-end systems, he began lobbying the board to consolidate global HR from six organisations into one team. In July 2025, he received the go-ahead and became vice-president for global HR services. Since then, his team has been focused on simplification, reducing total HR services from 1,100 to under 330.

“From onboarding to offboarding, we have owners for each of the different services, so we can have a team that’s solely focused on evaluating that. Where we need to be great, we are great, and where we just need to be good enough, making sure that we’re good enough,” he says. “And so that’s been our journey, continuing to look at how we optimise the organisation, provide a better employee experience, and simplify.”

Zaller has focused on five cultural components as he’s developed the HR team: being a changemaker, being future-focused, pushing continuous improvement, developing a “get-to-yes” attitude, and having a consultant mindset with a positive bent. “Those are what I really try to drive my team around and why I think we’ve been successful,” he adds.

Removing friction

Technology sits at the heart of this cultural mindset. Zaller says Cardinal Health’s digital transformation is about continuing the business’ growth trajectory.

“We’ve had a very nice run the last couple of years,” he says. “We have a simple, clean strategy. It’s about focusing on our businesses and our back-office approach. We want to create simplicity that allows the organisation to optimise and grow. My role in that approach is taking out friction and noise so the businesses can focus on growth.”

In his role, Zaller has led an organisational redesign focused on data hygiene, process optimisation and human-in-the-loop governance. Simplicity for HR means using emerging technology to help remove transactions. Last year, his team completed 50,000 tier-two transactions, where internal HR specialists process requests escalated from help desks.

“For the last mile, my team was taking information, punching it in, and then clicking go,” he says. “My team doesn’t need to do that. I don’t want them to do that. It’s mindless, boring, error-prone work. I’d rather have my team focus on our core 330 services, looking at what can be further optimised, and looking at what we need to do to make something great.”

“I’d rather have my team focus on our core 330 services, looking at what can be further optimised, and looking at what we need to do to make something great”

Adam Zaller, Cardinal Health

Zaller says the aim is to remove mundane tasks so that HR specialists act like consultants to the business. When professionals across the organisation call about an issue, his team has the time and space to act proactively and prevent organisational challenges from turning into employee relations concerns.

“I want to take friction out so that our managers and supervisors can spend more time on the shop floor with employees,” he says. “I want them to be there when an employee has a personal crisis or issue. That’s where I think I can help by simplifying what we do, so that we give more time back to our front line.”

Exploiting agents

Zaller recognises that agentic AI can help deliver the simplicity his business requires. While consultant PwC reports that 79% of executives say their companies are adopting AI agents broadly across business operations, adoption drops to 40% inside HR teams. Unlike slower-moving competitors, Cardinal Health is eager to exploit emerging technology.

Workday’s HR services provide the foundations for these explorations. The company went live with Workday in 2010 and has continued adding features. Under Zaller, the direction of transformation has been agentic. His organisation is using its solid foundations to create an AI-enabled approach to HR processes.

“We moved to the cloud early on,” he says. “We saw that having our data in the cloud and being able to move faster was a big part of how we were going to be a great HR organisation. That’s still the situation today. We’re close partners with Workday, so we have continued to add to the system.”

HR owns the Workday system, but the IT team helps maintain the implementation. Zaller’s team is currently exploring AI agents across key workflows, such as payroll processing and HR self-service. Cardinal Health manages high-volume recruitment of around 17,000 hires annually. Agents will help his team to manage these hires more effectively.

The first version of Workday Payroll Agent went live two months ago and helps HR professionals find anomalies in payroll data. The team is also testing Workday Self-Service Agent in a sandbox. Zaller expects this agentic service to help professionals eliminate many of the firm’s tier-one cases that are related to pay and time concerns.

“We went into our conversations with Workday with 30 or 40 use cases, and it got whittled down to only five because they’re adding so many skills into the Self-Service Agent,” he says. “I think that agent will be super popular and powerful.”

Aligning objectives

At the recent Workday Rising event in Las Vegas, the software provider discussed the 17 agents it has in production. While Zaller, who spoke to Computer Weekly at the conference, is eager to exploit these ready-made services, he’s also exploring how customised AI agents can help solve business challenges.

Cardinal Health was one of the first 40 companies to launch Developer Agent, which lets developers use natural language prompts to build custom apps and agents. The deployment went live in the summer. The HR team is using the approach to build a Comp Adjustment Agent to help manage the time-consuming process of workers’ compensation adjustments.

Zaller reflects on the agentic developments his firm has undertaken. “You’ll have a few agents that Workday provides that drive 80% of your stuff, and then there’s going to be 20% that’s custom to you, and you’ll want to use Developer Agent, and that’s perfectly fine,” he says. “I love how they’re giving us both options.”

A year or two from now, Zaller says his goal is for all Cardinal Health employees, regardless of country, to get all the information they need about people services, from onboarding to offboarding, in a very simple way on a mobile device.

“You would see a common front door for all HR services that every employee in the company can access, and HR to be a friction-free organisation that has predictable services,” he says.

What’s clear is Zaller wants his organisation to lead these technological advances. He’s committed to working closely with the IT department to meet these objectives. HR and tech teams must know their responsibilities and come together to create a common path forward.

“My peer on the HR IT side is at the conference,” says Zaller. “We are as aligned as aligned is going to get. He understands my strategy. He knows what he needs to do to help me achieve the goals. Last year, I wanted to go all in on AI, and he ended up doing a reorganisation to free up some roles to support my vision. That’s the best example of cross-functional teaming you can have.”

title: Italian court rejects data from police hacking of Sky ECC cryptophone network
raw_text:
An Italian criminal prosecution that relied on intercepted messages from an encrypted phone network, Sky ECC, which was infiltrated by French police, collapsed after a judge concluded the data should not be used as evidence in the case.

The trial in Catanzaro, involving more than 50 alleged members of a notorious Ndrangheta crime group in Southern Italy, led to acquittals for a majority of the defendants after a judge found that there was no evidence against them.

The case has raised questions about the admissibility of intercepted phone messages from encrypted phone networks used by criminals and whether defendants should be entitled to access raw data to prepare their defence.

Although the ruling has not set a legal precedent, defence lawyers argue that judges are likely to exclude evidence from Sky ECC in similar cases where defendants are unable to access the raw data used as evidence against them.

The judge excluded evidence from Sky ECC after finding that defendants did not have the ability to challenge the authenticity and reliability of the electronic evidence used against them, and that there was an absence of other evidence.

Man in the middle 

The court found in a 170-page verdict published this week that the charges against the defendants were based almost entirely on evidence obtained by French police by hacking the Sky ECC encrypted phone network in 2020.

French police, working with Dutch and Belgium police, attached a “man-in-the-middle” server to the Sky ECC infrastructure at the OVH Datacentre in Roubaix, France, to intercept messages and encryption keys.

Police in Italy issued three European Investigation Orders (EIOs) to obtain intercepted data from the French attributed to Sky ECC users in Italy, leading to arrests of suspected drug dealers and organised crime groups.

Defence lawyers questioned the integrity of the data supplied to Italy, which was delivered in the form of spreadsheets with missing metadata and missing messages, and did not meet forensic evidence standards.

In January, defence lawyers asked the court to issue an EIO requiring France to preserve evidence so that defendants could challenge the evidence against them in France. The French ignored the request.

Defendants had no legal remedy

The judgment found that the defendants had no legal remedy either in France or Italy to challenge the evidence used against them. It decided that the evidence should be disregarded where the defendants had no opportunity to comment on it or challenge it.

The court also found that there had been a lack of proper communication between France and Italy, and that France had handed over Sky ECC evidence to Italy without following the formal EIO route required by law. It acquitted 34 of the 50 defendants.

Commenting on the case, Dutch defence lawyer Justus Reisinger said: “In my opinion, the verdict is the only logical reasoning when confronted with cross-border intercepted evidence of which it is impossible to challenge in the country of origin.”

Defence lawyer Yehudi Moszkowicz said that the court had given the prosecution every opportunity “to be transparent about how the Sky ECC data was obtained, so that the defence could actually test it”.

He added: “That transparency never came – France refused, and the defendants were left with no forum anywhere to challenge the French collection. The judge drew the only lawful conclusion: evidence that cannot be tested cannot be used to convict.”

Moszkowicz stated that the ruling should serve as a “blueprint” for courts across Europe in other Sky ECC cases.

The European Court of Justice is expected to make a preliminary decision next week in a separate Sky ECC case following questions by the French supreme court over the circumstances in which EU states can accept evidence from another EU state.

The court will decide whether an EU country should be allowed to act on evidence supplied by another EU country if there is no mechanism in place to allow defendants to challenge the veracity of that evidence in the state that provided it.

title: Microsoft outage: Impact shows risk of M365 bundle lock-in
raw_text:
Several UK government departments, hospitals and schools have said they cannot send or receive email messages due to the global outage of Microsoft Exchange, which has impacted organisations that use Microsoft 365 products.

The Planning Inspectorate’s Manage Appeals Service said it has been temporarily paused for new submissions and customer access due to an email and system problem, and the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency claimed it has been experiencing issues sending and receiving emails, and that it has provided a phone number for urgent queries.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency also wrote that it was experiencing problems sending and receiving emails due to the worldwide Microsoft outage, but added that its search and rescue services have not been affected.

title: Government investigation into Post Office system too late for appeal against conviction
raw_text:
A government investigation into pre-Horizon systems used in Post Office branches will come too late for inclusion in a former subpostmaster’s appeal against a conviction based on one of the systems in the spotlight.

The Department for Business and Trade recently announced its planned investigation into systems used by subpostmasters before the controversial Horizon software at the centre of the Post Office scandal.

The government is yet to appoint a company to carry out the investigation and will not report until spring next year. But the appeal against the conviction of former subpostmaster Gareth Snow, in January, which Post Office is contesting, will cover the reliability of the Automated Payments Service (APS) and Automated Payment Terminal (APT) system. It has been confirmed that APT/APS are “among the systems the department intends the investigation to cover, alongside ECCO+, ALPS and ESNS”.

Cart before the horse

The subpostmaster’s legal team is seeking more information. Solicitor Neil Hudgell at Hudgell Solicitors, which represents Snow, said: “We welcome the review, but need to know more before we determine to what extent it impacts the progression of Mr Snow’s appeal.”

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which referred the appeal, has already said that the system which Snow used in his branch in Denbighshire “could cause accounting errors”.

Computer Weekly put to the government that the APT/APS appeal comes before the investigation and a spokesperson replied: “We are committed to getting to the truth about the impact of systems used before Horizon and continue to make progress towards appointing an independent investigator. We expect to confirm further details shortly.”

APT/APS is lesser known that Horizon and Capture, but was used by thousands of branches. In a 1994 news article in the Barry and District News, Richard Dykes, then managing director at Post Office Counters, was quoted as saying the APT/APS system was already installed in 3,000 Post Office branches, with the aim of reaching 6,000 over the following 12 months. It included an electronic terminal connected to telephone lines and was used to carry out transactions such as rent, rates and utility payments.

If Snow’s appeal is heard prior to the investigation report, it will not be based on a full picture, according to investigative scientist Ian Ross, a listed expert for the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague.

“Deciding an appeal weeks before a major state report on the exact same software is a psychological trap for the court,” he said. “Without the complete findings on APS/APT, judges are left anchoring their decisions to incomplete data – risking a verdict shaped by what is missing rather than what is true.”

Pre-Horizon problems

There are currently four former subpostmasters with appeals, due to be heard in the Court of Appeal, which blame systems that came before Fujitsu’s Horizon system for the unexplained losses they were blamed for.

The other three were Capture users, a pre-Horizon system that has already been investigated and found there was a “reasonable likelihood” it caused accounting losses. The Post Office is also contesting these.

Read Computer Weekly’s investigation of bug from 2015: Post Office IT support email reveals known Horizon flaw.

Snow’s appeal is due to be heard alongside the posthumous appeal former Capture user Patricia Owen, who died in 2003; and Steve Marston, a who ran a Post Office branch in Bury, Lancashire, which also used Capture.

The focus on systems used before Horizon has become necessary due to a huge body of evidence highlighting the Post Office’s treatment of unexplained shortfalls as the fuel behind the scandal. The arm’s length government body made subpostmasters take responsibility for unexplained shortfalls and kept quiet about its knowledge of bugs in the system that could cause discrepancies.

During a select committee hearing in January, the CCRC told MPs that there are 35 applications of interest, which it refers to as “pre-Horizon”. It said that any of these systems could be linked to miscarriages of justice, and it is not a giant leap to suggest that pre-Horizon software also caused unexplained shortfalls that subpostmasters were forced to cover.

There are 12 pre-Horizon cases currently being reviewed by the CCRC. A total of 40 pre-Horizon applications have been received in total, with 21 not referred to appeal, two withdrawn and four have already been referred. There was also a case that turned out to be related to Horizon and so was covered by legislation to overturn convictions.

A government investigation into pre-Horizon systems used in Post Office branches will come too late for inclusion in a former subpostmaster’s appeal against a conviction based on one of the systems in the spotlight.

The Department for Business and Trade recently announced its planned investigation into systems used by subpostmasters before the controversial Horizon software at the centre of the Post Office scandal.

The government is yet to appoint a company to carry out the investigation and will not report until spring next year. But the appeal against the conviction of former subpostmaster Gareth Snow, in January, which Post Office is contesting, will cover the reliability of the Automated Payments Service (APS) and Automated Payment Terminal (APT) system. It has been confirmed that APT/APS are “among the systems the department intends the investigation to cover, alongside ECCO+, ALPS and ESNS”.

Cart before the horse

The subpostmaster’s legal team is seeking more information. Solicitor Neil Hudgell at Hudgell Solicitors, which represents Snow, said: “We welcome the review, but need to know more before we determine to what extent it impacts the progression of Mr Snow’s appeal.”

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which referred the appeal, has already said that the system which Snow used in his branch in Denbighshire “could cause accounting errors”.

Computer Weekly put to the government that the APT/APS appeal comes before the investigation and a spokesperson replied: “We are committed to getting to the truth about the impact of systems used before Horizon and continue to make progress towards appointing an independent investigator.

title: Global Microsoft outage leaves users open to phishing attacks
raw_text:
Microsoft users globally have been unable to access services such as Outlook and Teams due to technical issues, which the company has described as “service degradation”.

The Microsoft Cloud status portal says users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services. The degradation of service impacts Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 Admin Center, Microsoft 365 applications, CoPilot 365, Microsoft Fabric, Defender, and Defender XDR and Microsoft Intune.

While most of the core functionality in Teams is unaffected, Microsoft warned that anything that relies on features like the Exchange Online calendar to schedule meetings is potentially impacted. 

For applications such as Power Apps, Microsoft said affected users may be able to use Power Apps or Field Service on the web as a way to circumvent impact. It also stated that users who are already signed in can potentially avoid impact by not signing out, clearing app data or reinstalling the software.

While there are plenty of reports that people have been unable to access their email, the degradation in service poses a big security risk for organisations that rely on Microsoft technology. For instance, the ability for organisations to manage device access is hampered due to the impact on Intune’s ability to handle device enrolment, device check-in and device compliance policies.

The fact that the usual channels of digital communications are affected means there is a window of opportunity for hackers to exploit the situation to gain unauthorised access to internal systems. At the time of writing, Microsoft said it was not aware of any malicious activity.

Speaking to Computer Weekly during the Gartner Symposium in Barcelona, Akif Khan, a senior director at Gartner, warned that employees can experience deepfakes in audio or video calls where people are impersonating executives, and try to trick those employees.

Download this podcast

“At the moment, a very common attack is one in which employees receive calls claiming to be from their IT service desk,” he said.

Khan warned that most organisations are behind the curve in terms of actually utilising the more forward-looking form of training that cyber security training providers are now offering. Such advances include training employees to identify phone-based phishing attempts by using deepfake phone calls.

Binalyze, which runs a cyber intelligence platform, argued that while security teams have been cut off from tools like Defender XDR or important alerts pushed via Outlook, attackers will be using phishing tactics as systems come back online.

Marie Wilcox, vice-president of market strategy at Binalyze said: “There are two risks. First, as services return, workers logging back in to their e-mail and clearing a day’s backlog are primed to trust anything that looks like it came from Microsoft. Fake security updates or requests to re-verify an account will land far more easily.
 
“Second, and harder to see, is activity that went unnoticed while alerts weren’t firing and nobody was watching the queue. A suspicious sign-in or a new inbox forwarding rule is easy to miss when everyone is focused on getting email back.”
